children: In wealth management, the roles that most shape client outcomes aren't always the ones with the flashiest titles. Team members who are technically in support roles can be instrumental in preventing mistakes, recognizing opportunities, and fostering client loyalty. For this week's Barron's Advisor Big Q, we asked team leaders to tell us about the easy-to-overlook contributions of those who don't sit in the advisor chair.

William Pitt, CEO, Evermay Wealth Management: Dana Tomisek, our chief operating officer, is rarely seen by clients, yet she's the reason each engagement with an advisor and a tax professional is so buttoned up and consistent at Evermay. We started as a very small firm, and we were only as good as each advisor and their team. Now we've built the firm to nearly 50 people, and we've leaned into workflows and our [customer relationship management system, or CRM]. Dana understands all the communication points: the spring and fall meetings and what will be covered, the custom communication sheets that go out to clients, the emails, and the meeting prep for each engagement, including tax and wealth management. She then systematizes all these data points into workflows in the CRM, so they are consistently utilized in every client meeting.

You would never see that, but you'd wonder why each of our advisory teams are so skilled and capable, not only with wealth management items but also with every bit of tax information you need to have a highly engaging, effective relationship with your tax preparer. Dana joined the firm four years ago as director of operations and client experience, and she was recently promoted to chief operating officer. For me, CRM used to be a fancy Rolodex and maybe a note taker. Now, with its workflows and communication, it does a whole lot more, and we are a much greater high-touch firm because of the technology she and her team know how to harness. Thanks to Dana, every client's experience is consistent.

Angelo Esposito Jr., founder, private wealth advisor, Harbor View Private Wealth: The role I'd point to is client service associate. It's easy to underestimate because the title sounds administrative, but on our team it has become central to client outcomes. My best example is Natalie Quinn. She started in that role in January, but her competency and organization made it clear she could take on more, so we built the position out with her.

Estate-planning integration is a good example. Natalie earned her CFP last year and is now working toward her Accredited Estate Planner credential, and she has become our liaison between clients and their estate attorneys. She leads many of the early high-level discussions-which is exactly the kind of conversation that used to fall through the cracks or wait for an advisor's calendar to open up. Now clients get faster, more coordinated answers, and the attorneys get someone on our side who actually understands the plan. It's a good reminder that "support" roles, done well, aren't just support at all. They're often the connective tissue that makes the whole client experience work.

Jim Dew, founder, CEO, Dew Wealth Management: I think immediately of Nellie Jess, our office operations manager. Most people from the outside would think she opens the door for the FedEx person, orders supplies and stocks the break room, stuff like that, but she does so much more. She always has the name up of anyone coming into the office; she knows the drink and snacks they like. She knows about their families and makes a great connection before any of our advisors go into the meeting. But she goes much further than that.

On one occasion there was a private-equity capital call and Nellie needed a client signature that day, but no one could get hold of the client. Nellie drove to her house but found it was a gated community and that she couldn't get in. So she climbed the fence, went to the house, knocked on the door. The client had turned all their devices off. She got the signature. The money got wired, and we avoided this big dilution for the client. We had a client in Texas who'd had significant tornado damage to their house. The advisor wanted to send flowers, but Nellie said, "No, no, no. Flowers are not what you send when someone is hit by a tornado." In 1980, the Nebraska town where she lived was devastated by a tornado. The thing everybody appreciated was when the Red Cross came by with food. So they looked up the notes on the client and found they loved steaks. We sent them high-end steaks, and this couple was so moved that they sent me emails saying, "We will never leave this firm, we are your clients for life."

Brad Johnson, co-founder, Triad Partners: I've coached independent advisors across the country for the past 20 years. One of the biggest disconnects I see in the space is when advisors don't deliver on the product that is being sold. They might say, "We build holistic financial plans to a CFP standard." But once you have an established book of business, you spend the whole week servicing and taking care of your people and growth stalls out. If you're more focused on growth, you're dropping the ball on delivering on the promises you made.

Clients want a plan that gets them where they want to be. They need income planning for when they leave their job, and they need an investment strategy that complements it. They need proactive tax planning. They need healthcare layered in there as they age. They need a legacy estate plan. And it's the service side that actually delivers all that. The person who does most of the back-end heavy lifting is typically a service advisor. A team-based approach including a service advisor allows you to scale and actually follow through on what you say you're going to do.
